blocks.text: There is a real difference between cleaning a dataset once by hand and building a cleaning process that reliably runs itself every time new data arrives. Most real world data pipelines need the second, not the first.
1. Why Manual Cleaning Does Not Scale

A script run once in a notebook, with cleaning steps chosen by eyeballing the specific dataset in front of you, breaks the moment a new batch of data arrives with slightly different quirks, and nobody remembers exactly what manual judgment calls were made last time.

It means wrapping the individual cleaning steps covered throughout this course, missing value handling, deduplication, standardizing formats, into REUSABLE FUNCTIONS with clear inputs and outputs, rather than inline code that only works on one specific dataframe.

A function is idempotent if running it twice on already clean data produces the exact same result as running it once, not corrupting the data further or throwing an error. This matters because a pipeline might occasionally reprocess the same batch, and idempotent functions make that safe rather than dangerous.

code.content:
cleaned_once = normalize_text_columns(raw_df, ['name', 'city'])
cleaned_twice = normalize_text_columns(cleaned_once, ['name', 'city'])
print(cleaned_once.equals(cleaned_twice))   # True, running it again changed nothing

def clean(df):
    df = normalize_text_columns(df, ['name', 'city'])
    df = fill_missing_numeric(df, 'age')
    df = drop_exact_duplicates(df)
    return df

clean_df = clean(raw_df)

blocks.title: An easy to forget practice
blocks.content: Having each cleaning function report what it actually changed, like "filled 12 missing values in column age" or "removed 3 duplicate rows", lets a human reviewing the automated run later see exactly what happened rather than trusting the output blindly.

code.content:
def fill_missing_numeric(df, column):
    df = df.copy()
    n_missing = df[column].isna().sum()
    median = df[column].median()
    df[column] = df[column].fillna(median)
    print(f"filled {n_missing} missing values in column {column} with median {median}")
    return df

blocks.text: 7. What Automation Should Not Try To Do

Judgment calls that genuinely require domain knowledge, like deciding whether an unusual value is a legitimate outlier or an error, are risky to fully automate without human review. Automation is best suited to mechanical, well understood, repeatable fixes, not every decision covered elsewhere in this course.

items: Writing a cleaning function that is not actually idempotent, silently corrupting data if it accidentally runs twice on the same batch.
Automating a judgment call that really needed human review.
Hard coding assumptions specific to one dataset into a function meant to be reusable across many.
Wrap each cleaning step as a function with a clear input and output.
Verify each function is idempotent by running it twice and comparing results.
Log what each function actually changed.
Reserve full automation for mechanical fixes, keep genuine judgment calls in human review.
